analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice suits at $250,000 and shields FDA-approved drug makers from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 229–196 on March 13, 2003, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten malpractice law nationwide. It caps compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how bad the injury, caps punitive damages, and gives injured patients only three years to file a suit after an injury shows up. It lets juries hear that an injured patient already has insurance covering some losses, caps lawyers' fees on a sliding scale, and bars punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved by the FDA, with exceptions if a company hid information from the FDA or bribed an FDA official. It would override state laws — but only state laws that give patients more ability to recover, keeping any state rules that protect doctors more.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers gain the most: damage caps and a shorter filing window directly cut the amounts they must pay out, and the bill's stated purpose is to lower malpractice insurance premiums. Drug and medical device makers gain a new shield — no punitive damages for FDA-approved products, and doctors who prescribe or dispense those products cannot even be named in a product liability suit, cutting off claims that might otherwise reach manufacturers. Patients who win suits keep full recovery of economic damages like medical bills and lost wages, and courts gain power to redirect more of a settlement away from lawyers to the patient.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Doctors, malpractice insurers, and drug makers

how_it_helps.text: It caps the amount doctors, hospitals, and insurers must pay for pain and suffering in malpractice cases at $250,000, which the bill's stated purpose is to use to lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce 'defensive medicine' costs.
It keeps full, uncapped recovery of economic damages — medical bills, lost earnings, and other out-of-pocket losses — for injured patients.

It bars punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products were approved or cleared by the FDA, and shields doctors who prescribe or fill prescriptions for such products from being named in product liability suits.
It limits lawyers' contingency fees to a sliding scale and lets courts supervise how settlements are paid out, aiming to direct more of any recovery to the patient.
It shortens the window to sue to three years from when an injury appears (or one year from discovery), making claims more predictable for providers and insurers.

analysis.who_pays: Injured patients and their families bear the cost: the $250,000 cap applies no matter how severe the injury, and it bites hardest where the harm is mostly pain and suffering rather than lost wages — children, retirees, and people who do not work for pay. The three-year limit can cut off claims that surface late, and the fee caps may make lawyers less willing to take difficult cases. States lose their ability to set stronger protections for patients, since the bill preempts state law unless the state rule protects providers more.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies no matter how severe the injury and regardless of how many defendants are liable, which falls hardest on patients whose losses are mostly pain and suffering — children, retirees, and people who do not work for wages, such as stay-at-home parents.

The bill bars punitive damages against manufacturers of drugs and devices that received FDA approval or clearance, unless the company withheld required information from the FDA or bribed an FDA official — so a patient harmed by an approved product could not seek punitive damages even if the company complied only technically with the rules.

The sliding cap on lawyers' contingency fees (40% of the first $50,000, down to 15% above $600,000) would make malpractice cases less profitable to pursue, and plaintiffs' attorneys say fewer lawyers would take harder cases, reducing injured patients' practical access to the courts.

The bill overrides state laws, but only in one direction: state rules are preserved only if they give providers and organizations more protection from liability than the federal bill does, so states that had guaranteed patients stronger remedies would lose them.

The claimed benefits — lower malpractice premiums, less defensive medicine, lower health care costs — rest on congressional findings in the bill itself, not on guarantees; whether insurers would pass savings to patients was not addressed in the legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would likely have reduced malpractice insurance payouts and could have eased premium pressure on doctors, and it preserved full recovery for out-of-pocket losses like medical bills and lost wages. But the costs fell on the people least able to bear them: a fixed $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages is worth the most to children, seniors, and stay-at-home parents, who have little or no lost income to claim, and the FDA-compliance shield would have removed a major financial deterrent against marketing unsafe products. The promised savings in premiums and health costs were asserted in the bill's own findings and are disputed. The bill was also written to preempt state laws, overriding states whose existing rules gave patients more room to recover. On balance, the protections it granted to providers and manufacturers were broader and more certain than the benefits it offered patients.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill in March 2003, but the Senate left it on its calendar and never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on March 13, 2003, by a recorded vote of 229–196, with 213 of 228 voting Republicans in favor and 186 of 205 voting Democrats opposed.

Before final passage, Rep. John Conyers offered a motion to send the bill back to committee with instructions to replace it with a 'Medical Malpractice and Insurance Reform Act of 2003'; it failed 191–234, with 189 of 205 voting Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on March 13, 2003, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 49; no further action was recorded.
The bill never received a Senate vote and died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005, leaving state malpractice laws unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients came out ahead: because the bill never became law, state malpractice laws — including states' own damage rules — remained in force, and drug and device makers did not get the federal punitive-damages shield. Doctors and malpractice insurers did not get the federal caps they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept full state-law remedies

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 213 of 228 voting Republicans voted yes while only 16 of 205 voting Democrats did; 7 Democrats were among the bill's 128 cosponsors.

industries.note: Caps on noneconomic and punitive damages and a shorter filing window directly limit the payouts insurers must make on malpractice claims. Whether the savings reached doctors' premiums or patients' costs is not addressed in the bill.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug and medical device manufacturers
industries.note: The bill bars punitive damages for products approved or cleared by the FDA and shields prescribers and pharmacists from being named in product suits, cutting off the liability chain to the manufacturer. Exceptions remain only if a company withheld required information from the FDA or bribed an FDA official.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and health care organizations
industries.note: Damage caps and a three-year filing deadline reduce malpractice exposure and insurance costs for providers. The benefit is partly entangled with patients' loss of compensation, though the bill argues lower premiums improve access to care.

A sliding cap on contingency fees (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000) and stricter punitive-damages pleading rules reduce the value and volume of malpractice cases. Their loss tracks the reduced recoveries available to injured patients.
